title: New Claude Limits to Prevent Game Cloning and Reverse Engineering
content:
Anthropic confirms new Claude Code limits to prevent game cloning — users report Opus 5.5 is also actively blocking reverse engineering tasks
Meanwhile, we now have direct reports of reverse engineering efforts being blocked, while online complaints grow.
Anthropic's recent move to have Claude Code deny video game cloning and possibly reverse engineering efforts has come under heavy fire from the software development community. Hot on the heels of Friday's report on the matter, an Anthropic employee responded to the tweet with the purported rule update with a direct statement confirming that the firm added guardrails to Claude Code to prevent game recreation.
In the full tweet, which you can read below, Addy Osmani says that "[Anthropic] added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against [its] usage policy." He goes on to state that work on original games is meant to continue working, and that Anthropic is iterating on the rules to try and "strike the right balance."
There's no telling what those sentences might be, though given Osmani's choice of words, it's possible that said sentences are indeed what X user Chasm posted a screenshot of: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."
In our previous report, we had already linked to recent issues raised at Claude Code's own GitHub repository, comprised of users complaining that the AI assistant was refusing to work on their games or on reverse-engineering tasks. As far as we can ascertain, it appears the game-related blocking is limited to the combination of using Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model. Should that prove true, then users should be able to sidestep the limitation by calling upon Opus using another harness like Ollama or forwarding specific requests through a wrapper of some sort.
Regarding the blocking of reverse engineering, we have received direct confirmations. The first comes from our own alumnus Jarred Walton, who was trying to run checks on the software he's developing. He notes that such work had been performed with no issue until yesterday, October 31, and that switching to Opus 4.8 let him continue his work.
Walton theorizes that Anthropic may have added a new rule to Code specifically for reverse-engineering. Considering that timing, plus the fact that other reports of refusals all popped up around the last week, may indicate that the company could be fiddling with cybersecurity-related rules in the same manner as they are for video game-related content.
We also received screenshots from a staffer's direct acquaintance, who asked Opus 5.5 (via Code) to try and reverse engineer a product activation, a request that likewise triggered safeguards. Meanwhile, notices that Claude Code appears to block reverse-engineering continue to mount, now with a Redditor allegedly having their account suspended, and then reinstated, over using Opus 5.5 and Reverse Engineer Anything. The company has an ongoing Cyber Verification Program, in which only approved entities get access to the full set of frontier models' cybersecurity capabilities.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

report.summary: Anthropic added guardrails to Claude Code's Opus 5.5 prompt blocking recreation of specific games and reverse-engineering tasks, sparking developer backlash.
report.background: Anthropic's Claude Code has become a popular agentic coding tool, and its Opus 5.5 model is used for everything from game development to binary analysis. AI-generated game clones and reverse-engineering have raised intellectual-property and cybersecurity concerns. Anthropic's usage policy already prohibits IP infringement, but enforcement was largely reactive. The update adds prompt-level guardrails that steer the model away from recreating specific existing games and, reportedly, from reverse-engineering tasks. The move comes amid growing scrutiny of AI coding agents and competition from open-weight and Chinese models that impose fewer restrictions. Anthropic also runs a Cyber Verification Program that gates advanced cybersecurity capabilities to approved entities, suggesting a broader tightening of security-related model behavior.
key_points: Anthropic employee Addy Osmani confirmed that two sentences were added to Claude Code's Opus 5.5 prompt to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game, citing IP infringement in its usage policy. Anthropic says original games, genre games, and games built from a user's own designs and assets should continue to work, and that it is iterating to balance the rules.

Users report the restriction extends beyond games. Tom's Hardware alumnus Jarred Walton said reverse-engineering checks that worked until October 31 were blocked, and switching to Opus 4.8 restored functionality. A request to reverse-engineer product activation also triggered safeguards. A Redditor allegedly had an account suspended and reinstated over using Opus 5.5 with a reverse-engineering tool.

The blocking appears tied to the combination of Claude Code and Opus 5.5 rather than the model alone. Reports suggest users may sidestep it by calling Opus through another harness such as Ollama or a request wrapper. That distinction matters because it points to prompt-level guardrails in Claude Code, not necessarily a hard model-level capability restriction.

The change has drawn heavy criticism on GitHub, X, and Reddit. Developers argue the rules are vague and could chill legitimate work such as security research, modding, preservation, and interoperability testing. Commenters note that competitors, including Chinese models, allow similar tasks and may capture market share if Anthropic restricts too aggressively.

Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program already limits full cybersecurity capabilities to approved entities, and the timing of reverse-engineering refusals suggests cybersecurity rules may be tightening alongside game-related ones. The lack of detailed public documentation leaves developers unsure where the line is, increasing frustration and encouraging workarounds.
report.impact: Anthropic's move signals that frontier AI labs will increasingly bake IP and security policy into model behavior, not just terms of service. For the AI industry, it sharpens differentiation: closed providers that enforce guardrails versus open-weight and Chinese models that do not. For developers, the practical effect is uncertainty—legitimate reverse engineering, security research, and game development may be blocked without clear appeal, pushing teams toward local models, alternative harnesses, and multi-model workflows. For regular users, fewer blatant game clones may be a modest positive, but the same filters could limit modding, preservation, and interoperability tools. The bigger risk is a chilling effect: if developers cannot predict refusals, they may avoid Anthropic tools for any work near IP or binary analysis, eroding trust and accelerating migration to less restrictive platforms.
report.tools: Watch Claude Code and Anthropic's usage policy updates; test alternatives like Ollama for local model hosting, OpenCode and Aider as open coding-agent harnesses, and Continue for IDE integration. For reverse engineering, legitimate workflows use Ghidra, IDA Pro, and Binary Ninja; pair them with models that permit the task. DeepSeek and other open-weight models are worth evaluating where policy allows. Always confirm licensing and authorization before reverse-engineering.
